metaTitle: Off-Page SEO: What It Covers, in Plain English
metaDescription: Off-page SEO is everything that builds authority away from your site. Here are the four activities that still register, and the six that stopped in 2012.
definition: Off-page SEO is the work done outside your own website — links, mentions, reviews and PR — that signals to search engines how much of the rest of the web trusts you.
answer: Off-page SEO is everything you do away from your own website to prove it deserves to rank: earned links, digital PR, reviews, and brand mentions people make without being asked. Four activities still count. Most of what Indian SEO courses teach in the off-page module stopped working around 2012.
takeaways: Off-page is not a synonym for link building. Reviews, unlinked brand mentions and branded search demand all sit in the same bucket.

Social bookmarking, directory submission, article directories, blog commenting and forum signatures have been dead since roughly Panda and Penguin — and are still on the syllabus at most Indian SEO institutes.
Digital PR is the modern core, because it's the only repeatable way to make a real publication want to link to you.
Measure it with new referring domains, review count and branded search impressions. Never with "submissions completed".

body: On-page SEO is everything on your side of the server: the words, the structure, the code. Off-page is the rest of the internet's opinion of you. You can edit the first one this afternoon. The second one has to be earned, which is why it costs more and takes longer.

Links are the loudest signal, not the only one. Anywhere your business appears without you paying for the placement counts: an editorial mention in a trade publication, 300 Google reviews with replies, a Reddit thread recommending you by name, someone typing your brand into Google instead of your category. Search engines — and increasingly the AI systems answering questions above them — assemble a picture of you from those sources and weigh it against the picture your own site paints.

Walk into most SEO training programmes in India and the off-page module still reads like it was written in 2010. Frequently it was. The tactics get taught, the interns get set to work on them, and a year later the client has a spreadsheet of 500 completed submissions and no additional customers.
Here's what actually became of each item on that list.

table.caption: Off-page tactics still taught in Indian SEO courses, and what happened to them.
head: Taught tactic
What actually happened
rows: The Open Directory Project (DMOZ) shut down in 2017. Most surviving general directories are link farms with a payment page attached.
Google's 2011 Panda update was aimed squarely at thin, syndicated article content. The rankings never came back, and neither did the directories that mattered.
Comment links are nofollowed by default on every mainstream platform. It's outreach with the volume turned down to zero.
A recognised spam signal since Penguin in 2012. Answering questions in a forum can still win you customers — the signature link isn't the reason.
The sites that carried weight are gone or unrecognisable. The "top 100 bookmarking sites" PDF still circulating in training WhatsApp groups is a museum piece.
Syndicated release links have been discounted for years. A release a journalist actually writes an article from is a completely different transaction.

callout.title: The ₹4,000 package
callout.body: "We'll submit your site to 500 directories." The submissions probably do happen. What you've bought is links from sites with no readers, no editorial process and often no index. At best it does nothing. At worst you spend next year cleaning up [toxic backlinks](/glossary/toxic-backlinks) instead of building anything.

body: Strip the syllabus back and four activities survive. They're harder, slower and less satisfying to report on, which is precisely why the dead ones persist.
bullets: **Earned editorial links.** A link inside an article somebody chose to write. The only repeatable engine for these is [digital PR](/services/digital-pr-services) — original data, expert commentary on something in the news, and a story a journalist can file before their deadline.

**Reviews.** For anything local or considered — clinics, restaurants, coaching centres, home services — Google reviews and the pace they arrive at are the off-page signal with the shortest path to actual revenue. They feed the local pack directly and they close deals on the profile before anyone reaches your website.

**Brand mentions, linked or not.** Search engines corroborate facts about an organisation across independent sources. A mention in a credible publication with no link still contributes to that picture, and unlinked mentions are frequently what AI assistants pull from when naming companies.
**Demand for your name.** People searching your brand rather than your category is off-page work compounding. It's the hardest signal to manufacture, which is exactly what makes it worth having.

sections.h2: How to tell whether any of it is working
body: Off-page is the easiest part of a retainer to fake, because the deliverables are activity rather than outcome. Five numbers make faking it difficult.
numbered: **New referring domains per month, with the list.** Not backlinks — see [referring domain](/glossary/referring-domain) for why the distinction matters so much here.
**Where those domains came from.** Named publications you could describe to your board, or a spreadsheet of sites nobody has heard of.
**Review count and average rating**, tracked per location, month over month.
**Branded search impressions** in Search Console. Filter queries containing your brand name and watch the trend across quarters, not weeks.
**Whether AI assistants name you** when asked the question your buyers ask. Crude, unstable, not a KPI — and increasingly the first thing clients notice.

callout.title: Where the hours go
callout.body: On a typical mid-size Indian retainer, off-page eats 20–30% of the hours and it's the part you cannot rush. We run [SEO from ₹75,000/mo](/pricing), and we'd rather ship four placements a quarter that a human being actually reads than 400 submissions a month that nobody does.

faqs.q: What is the difference between on-page and off-page SEO?
faqs.a: On-page is everything you control on your own site: content, titles, structure, internal links, speed. Off-page is everything that happens elsewhere — links, mentions, reviews, PR, branded search. You can fix on-page unilaterally. Off-page requires someone else to choose to reference you, which is why it's slower and more expensive.

faqs.q: Is off-page SEO just link building?
faqs.a: No, though links are the biggest component. Reviews, unlinked brand mentions, third-party profiles, community discussion and branded search demand are all off-page signals. For a local business, reviews often matter more than links; for a national B2B brand, editorial links usually matter more.

faqs.q: Do social bookmarking and directory submissions still work?
faqs.a: No. The bookmarking sites that carried weight are gone, and general directory links have been discounted for over a decade. They're harmless in small volumes and a liability in bulk. If an agency's off-page report is a list of submissions, you're paying for activity, not results.

faqs.q: How long does off-page SEO take to show results?
faqs.a: Links take the longest of anything in SEO to compound — typically three to six months before an improved profile shows up in rankings, longer in competitive categories. Reviews move faster, sometimes within weeks for local pack visibility. Plan off-page as the slowest track running in parallel, not as a sprint.

faqs.q: Can I do off-page SEO without buying links?
faqs.a: Yes, and you should. Original data, expert commentary, useful tools, genuine partnerships, review generation and being quotable are all unpaid. They're slower than buying, and they don't evaporate when a network gets deindexed.

faqs.q: How much of an SEO budget should go to off-page?
faqs.a: Roughly a fifth to a third of the hours on a mid-size retainer, with more in competitive national categories and less for a local business where reviews and Google Business Profile do the heavy lifting. If off-page is 60% of the budget in month two, ask what happened to the technical and content work.
